host.name: JP Smith
host.greeting: Hi, I'm JP! These are my personal favorites in the cities we visit. Tap a city to start.

cities.name: Memphis
cities.tagline: Home of the Blues & Birthplace of Rock 'n' Roll

stops.text: The Peabody Hotel for the famous Duck March.
Tour Sun Studio.
Rendezvous for dry-rub ribs, or the Arcade for Elvis's peanut butter and banana sandwich.
The National Civil Rights Museum.
Beale Street for live blues.
Graceland. Even non-fans leave changed.
The Rock 'n' Soul Museum on Beale Street.
Bass Pro Pyramid observation deck for the river view.

places.name: Charlie Vergos' Rendezvous
places.blurb: Since 1948 in a basement alley off Monroe Avenue. Charcoal-grilled dry-rub ribs with a secret Greek spice blend. The single most iconic meal in the city.

places.name: Arcade Restaurant
places.blurb: Memphis's oldest cafe, open since 1919. Elvis was a regular, and his grilled peanut butter and banana sandwich is still on the menu.

places.name: Central BBQ
places.blurb: Slow-smoked pulled pork and ribs in a sweet, tangy sauce. The pulled-pork nachos are a local obsession.
places.tip: Downtown location is next to the Civil Rights Museum.

places.name: Gus's World Famous Fried Chicken
places.blurb: Spicy, crispy fried chicken that's been called the best in America.
places.tip: Expect a short wait. Worth it.

places.name: Blues City Cafe
places.blurb: Fall-off-the-bone ribs and Delta tamales, with live blues nightly. One of the best values on Beale.

places.name: B.B. King's Blues Club
places.blurb: Great BBQ and live blues every night, named for the King of the Blues.

places.name: Beale Street
places.blurb: Designated by Congress as "The Home of the Blues." By night it's an open-air music festival.

places.name: Sun Studio
places.blurb: Where a teenage Elvis walked in in 1953 and changed the world. Johnny Cash, B.B. King and Jerry Lee Lewis recorded here too.

places.name: Stax Museum of American Soul Music
places.blurb: On the site of the original Stax studio: Otis Redding, Isaac Hayes, Booker T. & the MGs. Don't miss Isaac Hayes' gold-plated Cadillac.

places.name: South Main Arts District
places.blurb: Memphis's most walkable neighborhood: galleries, boutiques, cocktail bars and restaurants in old warehouses.
places.tip: Right next to the Civil Rights Museum.

places.name: Silky O'Sullivan's
places.blurb: Famous for the yard-long "Diver" drink and, improbably, live goats in the courtyard.

places.name: The Peabody Hotel Lobby Bar
places.blurb: Since 1933, live ducks have marched twice daily through the Peabody's lobby. Have a cocktail and watch.
places.tip: Arrive by 5 p.m. for the evening march.

places.name: Graceland
places.blurb: Elvis's home from 1957 to 1977. The Jungle Room, the Hall of Gold and the Meditation Garden. Fan or not, it's a must.

places.name: Memphis Rock 'n' Soul Museum
places.blurb: A Smithsonian creation tracing American music from the Delta cotton fields to the world stage. The audio tour has 100+ songs.

places.name: Bass Pro Shops at the Pyramid
places.blurb: A 32-story steel pyramid on the river with live alligators inside. Ride up to the observation deck for the best view in town.
places.tip: Observation deck has a fee.

places.name: National Civil Rights Museum
places.blurb: Built at the Lorraine Motel, ending at Room 306, where Dr. King was shot on April 4, 1968. One of the most important museums in America.
places.tip: Budget at least two hours.

places.name: Mason Temple & Mountaintop Memorial
places.blurb: Where Dr. King gave his final speech, "I've Been to the Mountaintop," the night before he died.

places.name: I Am a Man Plaza
places.blurb: Honors the 1,300 sanitation workers who struck in 1968. Their strike brought Dr. King to Memphis.

places.name: Slave Haven Underground Railroad Museum
places.blurb: Told Memphis's Underground Railroad story, with hidden spaces used to shelter freedom seekers.
places.closed: Closed after a fire. Check before visiting.

stops.text: Jackson Square, then beignets and chicory coffee at Café Du Monde.
Stroll the French Market, then ride the St. Charles streetcar through the Garden District (90-minute round trip).
Muffuletta at Central Grocery, a po'boy at Mother's, or Court of Two Sisters.
Mardi Gras World to see the floats being built.
A drink on Bourbon Street before dinner.
Frenchmen Street for live, authentic jazz.
The National WWII Museum. It deserves the whole day.

places.name: Café Du Monde
places.blurb: Since 1862. Beignets (square French doughnuts) and café au lait, 24 hours a day.
places.tip: Cash only.

places.name: Mother's Restaurant
places.blurb: Since 1938, famous for feeding WWII sailors. Home of the "World's Best" baked ham po'boy.
places.tip: Try the Ferdi Special.

places.name: Central Grocery & Provisions
places.blurb: Founded in 1906 by Sicilian immigrant Salvatore Lupo. The birthplace of the muffuletta sandwich.
places.tip: One sandwich feeds 2 to 4 people.

places.name: Acme Oyster House
places.blurb: A classic oyster saloon since 1910. Fresh Gulf oysters, raw or chargrilled.

places.name: Brennan's
places.blurb: Formal French Quarter dining since 1946, and home of the tableside-flamed Bananas Foster.

places.name: Antoine's Restaurant
places.blurb: America's oldest family-run restaurant (1840) and birthplace of Oysters Rockefeller. Fifteen ornate dining rooms.
places.address: 713 St Louis St, New Orleans, LA 70130

places.name: Court of Two Sisters
places.blurb: Daily Jazz Brunch in a lush courtyard on the site of a 1726 governor's mansion.

places.name: St. Charles Streetcar & Garden District
places.blurb: Running since 1835. The best way to see the grand Greek Revival and Victorian mansions of St. Charles Avenue.
places.address: Canal St & St Charles Ave, New Orleans, LA 70130
places.tip: Cash or app. $1.25 adults, 40¢ seniors, $3 all-day pass.

places.name: Magazine Street
places.blurb: Six miles of boutiques, galleries and local restaurants, from the Lower Garden District to Audubon Park.

places.name: French Market
places.blurb: Since 1791, the oldest continuously operating public market in the U.S. Souvenirs, crafts and food stalls.
places.address: 1008 N Peters St, New Orleans, LA 70116

places.name: Bourbon Street
places.blurb: Named for the French royal House of Bourbon. The heart of the late-night party scene.

places.name: Frenchmen Street
places.blurb: The "locals' Bourbon Street." The best place in town for authentic jazz, blues and funk.

places.name: Preservation Hall
places.blurb: Founded in 1961 to preserve New Orleans jazz. Intimate acoustic shows nightly in a rustic room.
places.address: 726 St Peter St, New Orleans, LA 70116
places.tip: Tickets required.

places.name: Fritzel's European Jazz Pub
places.blurb: In a pre-Civil War building, with classic, up-close traditional jazz.

places.name: Pat O'Brien's
places.blurb: A Prohibition speakeasy that invented the Hurricane. Dueling pianos and a flaming fountain courtyard.
places.address: 718 St Peter St, New Orleans, LA 70116

places.name: Tropical Isle
places.blurb: Inventors of the Hand Grenade, a sweet, strong and very festive tropical drink.

places.name: Lafitte's Blacksmith Shop Bar
places.blurb: Built between 1772 and 1791, one of the oldest buildings used as a bar in the U.S. Dark, candlelit and historic.

places.name: Mardi Gras World
places.blurb: The working warehouse where Mardi Gras floats have been built since 1947. See the artistry up close, year-round.
places.address: 1380 Port of New Orleans Pl, New Orleans, LA 70130
places.tip: 1-hour tour.

places.name: Audubon Aquarium
places.blurb: On the riverfront, with marine life from the Gulf to the Caribbean.
places.tip: Great on hot or rainy days.

places.name: The National WWII Museum
places.blurb: America's official WWII museum. Don't miss the Higgins boat, invented right here in New Orleans.
places.tip: Give it a whole day.

places.name: Sazerac House
places.blurb: An interactive museum of New Orleans cocktail history and the city's official drink, the Sazerac.
places.tip: Free. Bring a U.S. ID or passport.

stops.text: Tour the Ryman Auditorium, the Mother Church of Country Music.
Country Music Hall of Fame. Add the RCA Studio B tour if you can.
Hot chicken at Hattie B's, or whole-hog barbecue at Martin's.
The Johnny Cash Museum, then the National Museum of African American Music.
Lower Broadway honky-tonks: Robert's Western World and Tootsie's.
A show at the Grand Ole Opry.
Biscuits at the Loveless Cafe, or pancakes at Pancake Pantry.
The Parthenon in Centennial Park.
The Civil Rights Room at the Main Library, then walk past the Woolworth building.
Andrew Jackson's Hermitage.

places.name: Hattie B's Hot Chicken
places.blurb: Nashville hot chicken, the city's signature dish, at heat levels from mild to "Shut the Cluck Up!" The Midtown original opened in 2012.
places.tip: Expect a line. Start mild.

places.name: Prince's Hot Chicken Shack
places.blurb: Where Nashville hot chicken was born, run by the Prince family for generations. The legend says it began as revenge on a philandering Thornton Prince.
places.tip: Short on time? Prince's has an outpost downtown at Assembly Food Hall.

places.name: Loveless Cafe
places.blurb: Biscuits, country ham and homemade preserves since 1951, at the top of the Natchez Trace Parkway. They bake up to 10,000 biscuits on a busy day.
places.tip: About 25 minutes from downtown. Worth the drive.

places.name: Pancake Pantry
places.blurb: A Hillsboro Village breakfast institution since 1961, with a line out the door most mornings.

places.name: Martin's Bar-B-Que Joint
places.blurb: West Tennessee whole-hog barbecue, smoked low and slow, a short walk from Broadway.

places.name: Ryman Auditorium
places.blurb: Built in 1892 by riverboat captain Thomas Ryman as a gospel tabernacle, it was home to the Grand Ole Opry from 1943 to 1974. The Mother Church of Country Music.
places.address: 116 Rep. John Lewis Way N, Nashville, TN 37219
places.tip: Take the daytime tour, or better yet, catch a show from the old church pews.

places.name: Grand Ole Opry
places.blurb: The radio show that made country music famous, broadcasting since 1925. A circle of the Ryman's old stage floor is set into the stage.

places.name: Country Music Hall of Fame
places.blurb: The Smithsonian of country music: Elvis's gold Cadillac, Johnny Cash's guitars and the Hall of Fame rotunda.
places.address: 222 Rep. John Lewis Way S, Nashville, TN 37203

places.name: RCA Studio B
places.blurb: The studio where Elvis recorded more than 200 songs and the "Nashville Sound" was born.
places.tip: Visit only by tour, bought with Hall of Fame admission.

places.name: Johnny Cash Museum
places.blurb: The largest collection of Johnny Cash artifacts in the world, from his Sun Records days to the Man in Black.

places.name: National Museum of African American Music
places.blurb: Opened in 2021, it traces more than 50 genres from spirituals and blues to jazz, gospel and hip-hop. Very interactive.

places.name: The Bluebird Cafe
places.blurb: A tiny strip-mall club where songwriters play "in the round" and you hear the hits from the people who wrote them.
places.tip: Seats are reserved online and go fast.

places.name: Robert's Western World
places.blurb: Traditional country on Broadway in the old Sho-Bud steel guitar shop. Order the $6 Recession Special: fried bologna sandwich, chips, a MoonPie and a PBR.

places.name: Tootsie's Orchid Lounge
places.blurb: The purple honky-tonk where Opry stars slipped out the Ryman's back door for a drink. Willie Nelson and Patsy Cline were regulars.
places.tip: No cover. Tip the band.

places.name: Printers Alley
places.blurb: Once the heart of Nashville's printing trade, later a speakeasy alley. Neon, nightclubs and live blues today.

places.name: The Parthenon
places.blurb: A full-scale replica of the Athens original, built for the 1897 Tennessee Centennial Exposition. Inside stands a 42-foot gilded Athena.

places.name: Andrew Jackson's Hermitage
places.blurb: The plantation home of the seventh president, where Jackson and his wife Rachel are buried. A complicated, essential American story.

places.name: Civil Rights Room, Nashville Public Library
places.blurb: Sit at a symbolic lunch counter and read the Ten Rules of Conduct the students carried during the 1960 sit-ins. It overlooks the intersection where the protests happened.
places.tip: Free. Second floor, Special Collections.

places.name: Woolworth Building (Sit-In Site)
places.blurb: On February 27, 1960, a young John Lewis was arrested here for the first time, during the lunch-counter sit-ins. That May, Nashville desegregated its lunch counters.
places.address: 223 Rep. John Lewis Way N, Nashville, TN 37219
places.tip: Now a theater. View it from the sidewalk.

places.name: Fisk University & Jubilee Hall
places.blurb: In 1871 the Fisk Jubilee Singers toured the world singing spirituals to save their school. Jubilee Hall was built with the money they raised.
